p.title: Comparing Fine-Tuned RoBERTa with Traditional Machine Learning Models for Stance Detection in Political Tweets
p.venue: IECE Transactions on Advanced Computing and Systems

ext.title: Roman Urdu Stance Detection RoBERTa
ext.venue: IECE Transactions on Advanced Computing and Systems, Vol. 1, No. 2, pp. 78-96 (published 26 May 2025; submitted 24 Feb 2025, accepted 27 Apr 2025)
ext.document_type: Journal research article: empirical benchmark comparison of classifiers, with a newly built labeled dataset

ext.research_question: Can a fine-tuned RoBERTa model, and five traditional machine learning classifiers on TF-IDF features, classify stance (agree / disagree / unrelated) in Roman Urdu political tweets and replies, and which performs best? A secondary aim is to release a labeled Roman Urdu political stance dataset, since none was publicly available (Abstract p.78; Intro objectives p.80).
ext.theory: No explicit theory is tested. Stance is framed as a dialogic social act with evaluation, positioning and alignment, citing definitions attributed to "Kockelman" and "John" (pp.79-80). The task is modeled as three-class text classification (Fig. 1, p.80). No hypotheses are stated.
ext.data: Sample: 8,374 political tweets and comments (Abstract p.78). Table 1 (p.86) reports 8,373 rows and 11 columns, so the abstract and table differ by one row. Unit: a tweet-comment pair combined into one input sequence (p.92). Table 2 (p.87) shows example rows with tweet ID, comment, POS tags, named entities, dependency features, source, stance label and sentiment score. Labels: agree, disagree, unrelated. Source: Twitter API, keyword/hashtag search on Pakistani party and leader names (#ImranKhan, #NawazSharif, #PPP, #PMLN, #PTI; p.84). Collection period: not reported. Annotation: three annotators, with discussion to resolve disagreements; inter-annotator agreement described only as "substantial", with no statistic (p.84). Split: 80% train, 20% test (p.88). Test support is 1,675 (Agree 583, Disagree 602, Unrelated 490; Tables 3-7). The RoBERTa table (Table 8, p.93) reports support 6,699 on "the augmented dataset" (p.92), so RoBERTa and the classical models appear to be evaluated on different-sized sets. Data availability: "on request" (p.94).
ext.method: Preprocessing: stop-word removal, tokenization, POS tagging, lowercasing, lemmatization and phonetic spelling normalization (Section 3.3, pp.86-87). Features: TF-IDF for the classical models (pp.88-91). Classifiers: logistic regression (Eq. 5), decision tree with entropy/information gain (Eqs. 6-7), SVM with margin objective and kernel (Eqs. 8-10; kernel type not stated), random forest with majority vote (Eqs. 11-13; number of trees not stated), naive bayes (Eqs. 14-15). Deep model: RoBERTa fine-tuned on the concatenated tweet and comment, with a [CLS] classification head and softmax (pp.91-92). Dataset augmentation and class balancing are said to be applied (p.91), but the augmentation is described with image operations (rotation, flipping, color changes) and no text-augmentation procedure is given. Platform: Google Colab, Python (Section 4.1, p.88). Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (Section 3.6, p.87). No hyperparameters, epochs, seeds, cross-validation, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.
ext.identification: None. This is a descriptive benchmark on a single random 80/20 split of one dataset. No causal or quasi-experimental design is used.
ext.scope: Population: political tweets and replies in Roman Urdu (code-mixed, informal, multiple spellings) about Pakistani parties and leaders, drawn from Twitter (now X). Institution: none (not a government, party or legislative dataset). Era: collection dates not stated; published May 2025. Language scope: explicitly Roman Urdu, with claims about low-resource and code-mixed languages in general (Abstract p.78; Section 5 p.94).

key_findings.finding: Fine-tuned RoBERTa has the highest overall accuracy of the six models, on the augmented evaluation set.
key_findings.location: Table 8 p.93; Section 4.4.2 p.92; Section 4.5 p.93; Abstract p.78
key_findings.numbers: Accuracy 0.97; Agree P/R/F1 0.98/0.93/0.95; Disagree 0.95/0.99/0.97; Unrelated 0.96/0.99/0.98; support 6,699

key_findings.finding: Random forest is the best classical model, followed by SVM, logistic regression, decision tree and naive bayes.
key_findings.location: Table 6 p.90 (RF); Table 5 p.90 (SVM); Table 3 p.89 (LR); Table 4 p.89 (DT); Table 7 p.91 (NB); summary Section 4.5 p.93

key_findings.finding: Naive bayes is called the weakest model, 'close to random guessing'.
key_findings.numbers: NB accuracy 0.89. The majority-class share on the test set is about 0.36 (602/1,675), so the 'random guessing' wording is not supported by the reported numbers.

key_findings.finding: Computational cost is said to trade off against accuracy (RoBERTa costlier, RF cheaper), but no training time, memory or FLOP figures are reported.
Errors concentrate on sarcastic, ambiguous and implicit statements; some disagree items are labeled unrelated when negation is absent. No error counts or confusion matrix are shown.
Dataset augmentation and class balancing are credited with improving performance, but no with/without comparison is shown.
The paper claims a 97% result on an independent Twitter dataset, but that dataset is not described.
key_findings.numbers: 97% on an unnamed independent dataset; size and source not given

key_findings.finding: The F1 discussion leaves template placeholders unfilled in the text, next to the table.

limitations: Stated by authors: RoBERTa misreads sarcastic, ambiguous and indirect statements, and implicit disagreement (p.93). The authors call for sarcasm detection and better contextual embeddings.

Stated by authors: future work on other transformer architectures (XLM-R, XLNet, GPT-style and multilingual models) (pp.91, 94); hybrid stance plus fake-news classification; domain adaptation; cross-domain training with related low-resource languages; code-switching; a wider set of political topics; tools for other low-resource languages (p.94).
Stated by authors: BERT and LSTMs were excluded for lower accuracy on Roman Urdu and higher compute, but no numbers are shown (p.91).

Reader check, not an author claim: the dataset size is 8,374 in the abstract and 8,373 in Table 1. The test support of 1,675 for the classical models differs from the 6,699 support used for RoBERTa, so the models are not compared on one common test split.
Reader check: no inter-annotator agreement statistic (kappa or alpha) is reported; 'substantial agreement' is asserted only (p.84).
Reader check: no error bars, repeated runs, cross-validation or significance tests; a single 80/20 split with differences of 1-4 points between models.

Reader check: RoBERTa training details (learning rate, epochs, batch size, seed, max length) and classical hyperparameters (SVM kernel, RF tree count, TF-IDF settings) are missing, so the study cannot be reproduced from the text.
Reader check: the augmentation paragraph describes image operations (rotation, flipping, color adjustment) and gives no text-augmentation method (p.91).

Reader check: the Conclusion says all six models 'turned out as the best model' (p.94), which contradicts Section 4.5, and it mentions 'software repositories' (p.94), which does not match the Twitter political-stance task.
Reader check: collection period, retrieval date, keyword list completeness and sampling bias are not reported; the dataset is not public ('on request', p.94).

Reader check: reference-list errors. Yan et al. (ref [9], p.94) gives 2020 and 2018 in one entry. Ref [12] (Kavatagi & Rachh, a hate-speech paper) and ref [17] (Kucuk 2017, joint NER and stance) do not match the topics the text attributes to them, so the related-work citations need checking.
Reader check: no network, lobbying, persuasion, turnout or legislator analysis, and no election-outcome linkage; the political content is only the topic domain.
references_of_note: Walker, M. A., Anand, P., Abbott, R., & Grant, R. (2012). That is your evidence?: Classifying stance in online political debate. Decision Support Systems, 53(4), 719-729. Cited p.81; ideological debate stance, 4,731 posts; relevant to political text measurement.

Li, Y., Luo, Y., & Li, C. (2021). P-Stance: A large dataset for stance detection in political domain. Findings of ACL-IJCNLP 2021, 2355-2365. Cited p.82 and ref [18]; tweets from the 2020 US presidential election, the closest election-related stance benchmark in the paper.

Yan, Y., Chen, J., & Shyu, M.-L. (2018/2020). Efficient large-scale stance detection in tweets. IJMDEM, 9(3). Cited p.81 and ref [9]; 2016 US election tweets on Clinton and Trump; the citation entry has a year error.

Kucuk, D., & Can, F. (2019). A tweet dataset annotated for named entity recognition and stance detection. arXiv:1901.04787. Cited p.81 and ref [7]; Turkish tweet dataset with stance labels; relevant to dataset construction.
Kucuk, D., & Can, F. (2018). Stance detection on tweets: An SVM-based approach. arXiv:1803.08910. Cited p.82 and ref [19]; SVM-based stance on P-Stance-style data.

Ayyub, K., et al. (2021). Stance detection using diverse feature sets based on machine learning techniques. J. Intelligent & Fuzzy Systems, 40(5). Cited p.81 and ref [10]; direct comparison of classical classifiers with RNN, CNN-LSTM and DBN for stance.

Alturayeif, N., Luqman, H., & Ahmed, M. (2023). A systematic review of machine learning techniques for stance detection and its applications. Neural Computing and Applications, 35(7). Cited ref [6]; review of ML methods for stance.
AlDayel, A., & Magdy, W. (2021). Stance detection on social media: State of the art and trends. IP&M, 58(4). Cited ref [3]; survey of social-media stance detection.

Mets, M., Karjus, A., Ibrus, I., & Schich, M. (2024). Automated stance detection in complex topics and small languages: immigration in polarizing news media. PLoS ONE, 19(4). Cited ref [21]; low-resource-language stance on news media, with GPT-3.5 zero-shot.
Lan, X., Gao, C., Jin, D., & Li, Y. (2024). Stance detection with collaborative role-infused LLM-based agents. ICWSM 18. Cited ref [20]; LLM-agent zero-shot stance on SemEval-16, P-Stance and VAST.
Wang, X., et al. (2024). DEEM: Dynamic Experienced Expert Modeling for Stance Detection. arXiv:2402.15264. Cited ref [22]; LLM stance on P-Stance and MTSD (F1 81.1 and 83.4 per the text, p.83).

short_quotes.quote: Models such as BERT and LSTMs were excluded as they exhibited lower accuracy on Roman Urdu text
The Naïve Bayes classifier performed the worst, with an accuracy of 89%, which is close to random guessing.
The model achieved an overall accuracy of 97%, demonstrating superior performance in detecting stance from Roman Urdu tweets.

rel.summary_md:
Khan et al. (2025) built a Roman Urdu dataset of Pakistani political tweet-and-reply pairs, about 8,374 labelled agree, disagree or unrelated. They benchmarked five TF-IDF classifiers against a fine-tuned RoBERTa. Reported accuracy: random forest 0.95, SVM 0.94, logistic regression 0.93, decision tree 0.92, naive bayes 0.89, all on 1,675 test rows. RoBERTa reached 0.97, but on an "augmented" set with support 6,699, so it was not scored on the same test split as the others. There is one 80/20 split, with no kappa, no seeds, no hyperparameters and no confidence intervals. The augmentation is described with image operations (rotation, flipping), and the conclusion contradicts the results section. As evidence the paper is weak. The ranking gaps of 1 to 4 points have no error bars, and the transformer-wins headline is not a like-for-like comparison.

It still matters here because the system cites it as a method source. fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py is literally titled "Khan et al. pipeline". It copies the paired target-conditioned input, the five-classifier ladder, the class-balancing analog and the expectation that "transformer should beat all". fec/stance/stance_eval.py takes macro-F1 as its headline and adds "unrelated" as a class "per ICCK/TACS" practice. On Paul's own data the paper's two transferable claims did not hold. A transformer on the augmented press set scored 0.757 macro-F1, below a tuned word+char LinearSVC at 0.816. The Khan multi-view augmentation hurt the classical models and was rejected on 2026-07-03. The lasting value is in the evaluation conventions: "unrelated" as its own class, macro-F1 as the headline, and fine-tuning only once labels are clean. The model-ranking claims do not carry over. The code docstring repeats the paper's 0.93 to 0.97 figures as if they were faithful, comparable numbers. It should flag that RoBERTa was scored on a different test set.

bearings.paper_claim: Classical models on TF-IDF features rank RF 0.95 > SVM 0.94 > LR 0.93 > DT 0.92 > NB 0.89 (test n=1,675). Fine-tuned RoBERTa with tweet+comment paired input reaches 0.97 (support 6,699, augmented set). Augmentation and class balancing are credited with gains, but no with/without comparison is given.
bearings.system_side: train_stance_domain.py declares itself the Khan pipeline adapted to the CU domain. It builds a target-conditioned paired input ('target: X. speaker: Y. span + text'), runs the same five classifiers with class_weight='balanced', has an --augment flag that adds multi-view rows (title view and stance-span view, oppose rows upsampled) to TRAIN only, and has a --transformer path (distilroberta, 4 epochs, inverse-frequency loss weights).
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py:3-13 (docstring cites the paper and restates its accuracies), :31-34 (paired input), :42-59 (Khan multi-view augmentation), :94-103 (five-model ladder; prints 'Khan et al. ordering ... transformer should beat all'), :120-127 (class-weighted RoBERTa loss)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper had about 8k labels in one language and one domain, a single split, and RoBERTa scored on a different and larger test set. The system has 456 train / 87 test press rows with a never-reshuffled split. The mechanics transfer (paired input, balanced loss). The model ordering and the augmentation benefit do not: neither is tested like-for-like in the paper, and both failed here.

bearings.paper_claim: The transformer beats every classical model (0.97 vs at most 0.95), and dataset augmentation and balancing improve performance.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.4.2 p.92; Section 4.5 p.93; Abstract p.78
bearings.system_side: On the CU press gold set, the transformer trained on augmented data reached 0.757 macro-F1, below the tuned word+char LinearSVC at 0.816 (83.9% acc, untouched test n=87). Brain note 2026-07-02 says augmenting the same 456 rows cannot close the gap; new labels are needed. On 2026-07-03, 'Khan augmentation HURTS classical (rejected)'. Production is the SVM, not a transformer.
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py:26,42-59 (--augment path, now rejected); fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py:78-92 (tune path that produced the production SVM)
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are system results, single-look on an 87-row test (about +/-8.5% CI), so they are UNVERIFIED by a second path (DE-062). They show that the paper's ordering does not carry to small English congressional press corpora. The paper's own comparison is also confounded (different test supports), so neither result settles the general question.

bearings.paper_claim: Stance is a three-way task in which 'unrelated' is a first-class label alongside agree and disagree. The paper reports per-class precision, recall and F1 with macro averages.
bearings.system_side: The S1 evaluation harness scores any prediction column against adjudicated gold, with macro-F1 as the headline 'per ICCK/TACS.2025.928069 practice'. Its class set includes 'unrelated'. The tweet trainer uses the same four classes, and its headline is 5-fold CV rather than one split.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This transfers fully. Labelling and metric conventions do not depend on language or domain. The system goes further than the paper by using CV for small n and slice breakdowns. The paper itself gives no CV, no agreement statistic and no CI, so it is a source for the convention only, not for validation rigor.

bearings.paper_claim: A fine-tuned RoBERTa reaches 0.97 accuracy on political stance, with errors concentrated in sarcastic, ambiguous and implicit statements, and implicit disagreement mislabelled as unrelated.
bearings.system_side: The production transformer reader is Political DEBATE NLI, fine-tuned on 552 rows for 3 epochs. It scores 0.839 acc / kappa 0.742 held out and 0.571 on the adversarial goldeval frame. A tuned SVM ties it (0.835 macro-F1). The recorded dominant error is implicit support read as neutral (n=78).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 0.97 headline should not be used as a target or prior. It comes from about 8k in-domain labels and a non-common test set. The error-mode finding (implicit and indirect stance) does transfer, and it matches the system's neutral/support seam. Treat the paper as weak, qualitative support only.

gaps_exposed: The paper's one usable pointer is that implicit and indirect stance is the residual failure. The system knows its dominant error (implicit support read as neutral, n=78), but it has no dedicated handling for implicit stance or sarcasm in either the SVM or DEBATE readers.

The production press classifier (stance_clf_composed.pkl) still has no 'unrelated' class (07-03 note), although the evaluation harness and tweet trainer treat 'unrelated' as first-class. Training and evaluation label spaces are mismatched on the press side.

train_stance_domain.py lists the paper's accuracies as a faithful baseline and expects 'transformer should beat all'. The docstring does not record that the paper scored RoBERTa on a different test support (6,699 vs 1,675), or that the system's own result reversed the ordering. A reader of the code would inherit an unsupported expectation.
flags: The code comment at fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py:103 ('transformer should beat all') and the docstring at :5-8 present the paper's model ordering as established. The paper's RoBERTa and classical results come from different test sets, and the system measured the opposite (0.757 vs 0.816 macro-F1). This is a stale or unsupported expectation embedded in code, not a validated prior.

Brain notes conflict on the augmentation history. The 2026-07-02 note credits '--augment (Khan multi-view)' plus tuning with the 83.9% / 0.816 result. The 2026-07-03 note says Khan augmentation hurts classical models and was rejected, with tune-only reaching 0.835. The component description follows the 07-03 version. Any citation of the 0.816 figure should state which configuration produced it.

Any quote of the paper's 0.97 must name its denominator: support 6,699 on the 'augmented dataset', not the 1,675-row test used for the classical models. The paper's own 'close to random guessing' claim for naive bayes at 0.89 is false against a majority-class share of about 0.36.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's annotated position, from Birkenmaier and Kim J. 2025, favours transformers and LLMs over bag-of-words SVMs. His highlights call SVM baselines outdated. This paper looks as if it supports that view, but its comparison is confounded, and the system's own measurements on CU press data (552 labels) went the other way. A tuned word+char LinearSVC tied or beat the fine-tuned transformers: 0.816 vs 0.757 macro-F1 for distilroberta, and 0.835 vs 0.839 against DEBATE. The LLM and API readers did beat the classical model on tweets (Opus 0.662 vs transfer 0.357 F1). So Paul's preference holds for large LLMs, not for small fine-tuned encoders on a few hundred labels. His notes do not record that outcome, and on this point they are stale relative to the system. His flagged weakness, ambiguous statements, matches the paper's stated error mode.

related.why: Ornstein evaluates LLMs on political text with small labelled sets. That is the regime where the system's evidence (LLM readers beat small fine-tuned encoders) diverges from Khan's large-label RoBERTa result.
Dai uses LLM-enhanced stance detection aimed at implicit and reasoning-dependent stance, which is the failure mode Khan reports but does not address.
Another lexical/classical stance-direction approach the system tried and rejected (3 good / 43 bad sign changes). Together they document why the classical-feature route was bounded in this domain.

Birkenmaier reports GPT-4o beating SVM and XLM-R with proper validation (Krippendorff alpha, macro-F1). Khan reports transformer superiority without comparable rigor. Paul's transformer preference rests on Birkenmaier, not on this paper.
Rice and Zorn's domain dictionaries are the lexical baseline lineage behind the legacy scorer. Khan's TF-IDF ladder is the supervised-classical step above it in the same stack.
